title: Acts 28:1–16
context: The survivors find themselves on Malta, where the islanders show unusual kindness and build a fire. A viper fastens on Paul’s hand, and the islanders think he is a murderer pursued by justice, but when he shakes it off unharmed, they decide he is a god. Paul heals the father of Publius, the chief official, and many other sick islanders, and they honor the travelers and supply their needs. After three months they sail on to Italy, believers from Rome come out to meet them, and Paul thanks God and takes courage. In Rome he is allowed to live by himself with a soldier guarding him.

verses.text: When we had escaped, then they learned that the island was called Malta.
verses.arminianNotes: Once safe, they learn the island is Malta, called Melita in the text.
verses.reformedNotes: Malta lay on the grain route to Italy, so a ship bound for Rome would eventually call there.

verses.text: The natives showed us uncommon kindness; for they kindled a fire and received us all, because of the present rain and because of the cold.
verses.arminianNotes: The islanders, whom Luke calls barbarians simply because they did not speak Greek, show unusual kindness and build a fire against the rain and cold.
verses.reformedNotes: Kindness from strangers outside the faith is a recurring note in Acts. Reformed theology calls this common grace, God’s goodness working through people who do not yet know him.

verses.text: But when Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and laid them on the fire, a viper came out because of the heat and fastened on his hand.
verses.arminianNotes: Paul gathers a bundle of sticks and lays them on the fire, and a viper driven out by the heat fastens on his hand.
verses.reformedNotes: The apostle is collecting firewood with everyone else. Luke shows him serving, not being served.

verses.text: When the natives saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, “No doubt this man is a murderer, whom, though he has escaped from the sea, yet Justice has not allowed to live.”
verses.arminianNotes: The islanders say he must be a murderer whom Justice, the goddess Dike, will not allow to live even though he escaped the sea.
verses.reformedNotes: Pagan conscience assumes a moral order in which guilt catches up with the guilty.

verses.text: However he shook off the creature into the fire, and wasn’t harmed.
verses.arminianNotes: Paul shakes the creature into the fire and suffers no harm, as Jesus promised his messengers in Luke 10:19.
verses.reformedNotes: God’s protection continues on land as it did at sea. The promise of 23:11 still governs events.

verses.text: But they expected that he would have swollen or fallen down dead suddenly, but when they watched for a long time and saw nothing bad happen to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god.
verses.arminianNotes: They wait for him to swell up or drop dead, and when nothing happens, they change their minds and say he is a god.
verses.reformedNotes: The same crowd moves from murderer to god in moments, much as the Lystrans did in 14:11–19.

verses.text: Now in the neighborhood of that place were lands belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius, who received us and courteously entertained us for three days.
verses.arminianNotes: Nearby are estates belonging to Publius, the island’s chief official, who welcomes them and entertains them hospitably for three days.
verses.reformedNotes: Inscriptions confirm that “first man” was the official title of Malta’s leading magistrate.

verses.text: The father of Publius lay sick of fever and dysentery. Paul entered in to him, prayed, and laying his hands on him, healed him.
verses.arminianNotes: Publius’s father lies sick with fever and dysentery. Paul visits, prays, lays hands on him, and heals him.
verses.reformedNotes: Luke, a physician, uses precise medical terms. Paul prays before laying on hands, making clear the healing comes from God.

verses.text: Then when this was done, the rest also who had diseases in the island came and were cured.
verses.arminianNotes: After this, others on the island who have diseases come and are cured.
verses.reformedNotes: Luke records no preaching here, though the healings in Jesus’ name surely carried the message.

verses.text: They also honored us with many honors; and when we sailed, they put on board the things that we needed.
verses.arminianNotes: They honor the travelers in many ways and, when it is time to sail, supply what they need.
verses.reformedNotes: God provides for the shipwrecked company through the gratitude of the islanders.

verses.text: After three months, we set sail in a ship of Alexandria which had wintered in the island, whose figurehead was “The Twin Brothers.”
verses.arminianNotes: After three months they sail on an Alexandrian ship that had wintered at the island, with the Twin Brothers, Castor and Pollux, as its figurehead.
verses.reformedNotes: The pagan sailors’ patron gods ride on the prow, while the God who actually kept them safe is the one Paul serves.

verses.text: Touching at Syracuse, we stayed there three days.
verses.arminianNotes: They put in at Syracuse in Sicily and stay three days.
verses.reformedNotes: The voyage now follows the regular grain route toward Italy.

verses.text: From there we circled around and arrived at Rhegium. After one day, a south wind sprang up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli,
verses.arminianNotes: From there they sail around to Rhegium, at the toe of Italy, and with a south wind reach Puteoli in two days.
verses.reformedNotes: Puteoli, near Naples, was the main port for grain ships before Ostia was expanded.

verses.text: where we found brothers, and were entreated to stay with them for seven days. So we came to Rome.
verses.arminianNotes: At Puteoli they find believers and are invited to stay seven days. “And so we came to Rome.”
verses.reformedNotes: The gospel had already reached Italy before Paul. He arrives to find brothers waiting.

verses.text: From there the brothers, when they heard of us, came to meet us as far as The Market of Appius and The Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, he thanked God and took courage.
verses.arminianNotes: Believers from Rome come as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns, about forty and thirty miles out, to meet them. Seeing them, Paul thanks God and takes courage.
verses.reformedNotes: Paul had written to these believers years earlier (Romans 1:11–12). The encouragement he hoped to give, he first receives.

verses.text: When we entered into Rome, the centurion delivered the prisoners to the captain of the guard, but Paul was allowed to stay by himself with the soldier who guarded him.
verses.arminianNotes: In Rome Paul is allowed to live by himself with a soldier guarding him.
verses.reformedNotes: God’s word in 23:11 is fulfilled. The prisoner has reached the capital exactly as promised.
